title: What is the difference between an API (the contract/interface a service exposes) and an SDK (a client library wrapping that API with language-specific helpers, auth, retries, serialization)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between an API and an SDK
keyPoints: The API is the language-neutral contract a service exposes: endpoints, request/response shapes, status codes, and authentication rules.
The SDK is a language-specific client library that wraps the API with typed methods, auth handling, retries, and serialization.
The SDK depends on the API; the API can exist without any SDK, but an SDK cannot exist without an API to wrap.
One API often has many SDKs, one per language (Java, Python, Go), all talking to the same contract.
SDKs speed up integration and reduce mistakes but add a dependency that must track API versioning.
In regulated banking, teams sometimes call the raw API directly for full auditable control over every byte sent.

s1_definition.oneliner: The API is the language-neutral contract a service exposes; the SDK is a language-specific library that wraps that contract with auth, retries, serialization, and typed methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **API (Application Programming Interface)** – the contract a service exposes: endpoints, request/response schemas, status codes, headers, and authentication rules, independent of any programming language.
- **SDK (Software Development Kit)** – a language-specific client library that wraps the API, providing typed methods, automatic auth handling, serialization/deserialization, retries with backoff, and error mapping.
- **Relationship** – the SDK is built on top of the API; one API can have many SDKs (Java, Python, Go), all talking to the same contract.
- **Trade-off** – SDKs speed integration but add a versioned dependency; calling the raw API gives maximum control.
s1_definition.analogy: The API is the official rulebook of National Bank of India: to transfer money, send a form of this exact shape to this counter, and you will get back a receipt of this shape. Anyone who can read the rulebook can transact, in any language. The SDK is a personal bank assistant who already knows the rulebook by heart. You say "transfer fifty thousand to Priya" and the assistant fills the correct form, stands in the right queue, retries if the counter is busy, and hands you back the receipt.

```text
  API vs SDK:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   API Contract                   │
  │  POST /api/v1/transfers                          │
  │  { from, to, amount } → { transferId, status }   │
  │  Status codes: 201, 400, 401, 404, 500           │
  └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        │            │            │
  ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌───┴─────┐ ┌───┴──────┐
  │ Java SDK  │ │Python SDK│ │  Go SDK  │
  │ .create() │ │.create() │ │.Create() │
  │ auth      │ │ auth     │ │ auth     │
  │ retries   │ │ retries  │ │ retries  │
  │ types     │ │ types    │ │ types    │
  └───────────┘ └─────────┘ └──────────┘

  Each SDK wraps the same API contract for its language.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An API is the contract a service exposes: the endpoints, request and response shapes, status codes, headers, and authentication scheme. It is language-neutral, so a client in Java, Python, Go, or plain curl all interact with exactly the same agreement, usually documented with OpenAPI. An SDK is a language-specific library that wraps that API and hides the mechanics: instead of hand-building URLs, attaching tokens, serializing JSON, and implementing retries, the developer calls a single typed method.

The SDK adds authentication handling that refreshes tokens automatically, serialization so you work with typed objects, error mapping so an HTTP 404 becomes a catchable exception, and resilience features like retries with exponential backoff. The relationship is one-directional: the SDK depends on the API, the API exists without any SDK, and one API commonly has many SDKs, one per language.

At National Bank of India, the team exposed a payments API to fintech partners and shipped a Java SDK. A partner integrating against the raw API had to write boilerplate for every call and kept making mistakes like forgetting token refresh. With the SDK they called one method and auth, JSON, retries with an idempotency key, and error mapping were all handled. Their Python and Go teams each got their own SDK wrapping the identical contract.

The trade-off to keep in mind is that an SDK speeds integration but adds a dependency to maintain, can lag behind the newest API features, and hides behavior like retry policy that you may need to tune. For a public API, provide both the raw contract and official SDKs. In highly regulated banking integrations, sometimes call the raw API directly for full auditable control.

Remember one sentence: the API is the rulebook everyone reads, and the SDK is the assistant who knows it by heart and fills out the forms for you.
